passages.t: Tomorrow, honest wounds, and a neighbor nearby
passages.happening:
“Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring” (verse 1). Let someone else praise you, not your own mouth (verse 2). ‘A stone is heavy and sand is a burden, but aggravation from a fool outweighs them both’ (verse 3). Wrath is cruel and anger a flood, ‘but who can withstand jealousy?’ (verse 4).

Then sayings about friendship. ‘Better an open rebuke than love that is concealed’ (verse 5). “The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful” (verse 6). ‘Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who wanders from his home’ (verse 8). ‘Oil and incense bring joy to the heart, and the sweetness of a friend is counsel to the soul’ (verse 9).

Do not abandon your friend or your father's friend, and in a day of trouble ‘better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
After the portraits of fools and slackers in chapter 26, this chapter turns to relationships: friends, neighbors, brothers, and a father's hopes for his son. It is one of the warmest chapters in Proverbs, and several of its sayings have become part of ordinary speech.

Verses 5 and 6 say something surprising. A friend who tells you a hard truth is showing love, and the wound is a faithful one. An enemy's kisses, all warmth on the outside, cannot be trusted.

Friendship in the ancient world carried obligations that could pass from one generation to the next. A father's friend was a relationship you inherited, like land. In small communities with no police or social services, a neighbor close at hand could do more in a crisis than a brother far away.
passages.later: James takes up verse 1 for those who plan their year of business: “You do not even know what will happen tomorrow!” (James 4:14). The law made honest rebuke a duty of love: ‘Directly rebuke your neighbor, so that you will not incur guilt on account of him’ (Leviticus 19:17). And the prophet Nathan gave David the faithful wound of verse 6 (2 Samuel 12:7).
passages.asks: The wounds of a friend are faithful. Ask who loves you enough to tell you the truth, and whether you let them. And ask whether you have plans for tomorrow that you are boasting about as if they were already yours.

passages.t: Iron sharpens iron, and the heart in the water
passages.happening:
‘Be wise, my son, and bring joy to my heart, so that I can answer him who taunts me’ (verse 11). ‘The prudent see danger and take cover’ (verse 12).

A loud greeting early in the morning can be counted as a curse (verse 14). ‘A constant dripping on a rainy day and a contentious woman are alike’ (verse 15), and holding her back is like holding back the wind or grasping oil (verse 16).

“As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another” (verse 17). ‘Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit’ (verse 18). “As water reflects the face, so the heart reflects the true man” (verse 19). Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and neither are human eyes (verse 20). Silver and gold are tested in the fire, ‘but a man is tested by the praise accorded him’ (verse 21). Even if a fool is ground like grain in a mortar, his folly will not leave him (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Verse 14 is a funny picture of a neighbor who means well and annoys: a loud greeting at dawn, and the person greeted counts it a curse. Good words need good timing.

Verses 15 and 16 repeat a picture from 19:13. They describe how hard life is in a home without peace. They are not a comment on women in general. The book calls a prudent wife a gift from the LORD (19:14).

Iron sharpening iron suggests friction that makes both sides better, though some note that sharpening can also describe a hard, even heated, exchange.

Sheol and Abaddon are names for the realm of the dead, pictured as never full. The human eye is the same: always wanting more.

Verse 21 adds something to 17:3. The metalworker tests silver in the fire. A person is tested by praise. How someone handles being admired shows what they are made of.
passages.later: Hebrews speaks of the same kind of friendship as verse 17: ‘And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds’ (Hebrews 10:24). And Ecclesiastes agrees with verse 20: ‘the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing’ (Ecclesiastes 1:8).
passages.asks: As iron sharpens iron, one person sharpens another. Ask who sharpens you, and whom you sharpen. And ask how you handle praise, since verse 21 says it tests a person as fire tests silver.

passages.t: Know the condition of your flocks
passages.happening:
The chapter ends with a short poem. ‘Be sure to know the state of your flocks, and pay close attention to your herds’ (verse 23), ‘for riches are not forever, nor does a crown endure to every generation’ (verse 24).

When the hay is cut and new grass appears, and the grain is gathered from the hills, ‘the lambs will provide you with clothing, and the goats with the price of a field’ (verse 26). There will be goats' milk enough to feed the household and the servants (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
This is the longest single unit in chapters 25 to 29. It describes the pastoral life of Judah's hill country: wool for clothing, goats sold to buy land, milk to feed the family and its servants.

The poem is about steady faithfulness. Money comes and goes, and even crowns do not last. But a household that knows and tends what it has will be provided for.

Because the poem follows a line about crowns, many readers hear it as advice for rulers as well as herders. A king, like a shepherd, should know the condition of those in his care.
passages.later: Peter gives the same charge to the church's leaders: ‘Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you’ (1 Peter 5:2).
passages.asks: Know the condition of your flocks. Ask what has been entrusted to your care, at home, at work or in your church, and whether you know how it is really doing. And ask what you are counting on that, like riches and crowns, will not last.
